baseline_incident_edges.relationship: places women’s rights organizing alongside labor and Black women’s activity before the 1960s
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: James and Rupp identify broader coverage while offering different criticisms. Later women’s history is neither a uniform continuation nor a field founded by this book alone. Original 1959 text and later editions remain distinct.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Rights organizing, labor and archival reach

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: makes women’s rights organizing an object of political history while exposing disputed movement boundaries
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Ostrander questions causal integration of other reforms; Rupp distinguishes historical self-definition from broadened categories. These receptions clarify the political-history contribution without settling the disagreement.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Black historical collections and Terrell’s papers supply documentary resources for Flexner’s wider coverage
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Rupp p. 163 identifies Schomburg, Howard and Terrell collections in Flexner’s bibliography. This is mediated evidence of documentary use, not direct personal advice, consultation of those archives here or a claim that Black women’s activity was fully covered.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Schomburg, Howard and Terrell documentary resources

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Rupp questions the limits of movement categories and the absence of private relationships in Flexner’s account
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Available 1992 passages value the inclusion of Black and white working women while questioning other exclusions and distinguishing historical self-identification from broader collective activity. Missing preview pages are not inferred; this is later reception.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Ostrander questions suffragist self-definition and the causal integration of other reforms
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The complete review recognizes extensive research and Flexner’s narrower stated aim while examining abolition, temperance and evangelical support. His criticism is a specific intervention, not the position of all political historians.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Frances James asks for a structural explanation through private property and a program beyond reform
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1960 review also welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage. This particular Marxist criticism does not make the book devoid of explanation, identify James with Janet Wilson James or establish a uniform Marxist response.
